PRINTABLE STAFF STRATEGY GUIDES

One useful technique on one page

80 practical guides organised around the BSCS model. Read online, print a PDF or edit the Word version. Each includes steps, teacher language, a classroom example, five top tips and linked further reading.

Complete PDF collection ↓Editable collection ↓All individual files ↓

Choose a useful next step for the learning problem. These are a menu, not a checklist for every lesson. Agreed BSCS routines retain their status as school expectations; other techniques are practitioner guidance.

80 guides

LP01 · Lesson Preparation

Planning backwards from what students need to learn

Use this when a lesson contains worthwhile activities but the knowledge students should leave with is unclear. Start with the intended learning, then select the explanation, practice and checks that will build it.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
LP02 · Lesson Preparation

Prerequisite knowledge checks: identifying the foundations for new learning

Use this before new teaching when students need specific existing knowledge to access the explanation. Check the actual prerequisite rather than asking whether students remember last lesson.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
LP03 · Lesson Preparation

Anticipating misconceptions and planning how to uncover them

Use this when students repeatedly make the same plausible error. Anticipate the reasoning behind that error so the lesson exposes and repairs it rather than merely announcing the correct answer.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
LP04 · Lesson Preparation

Diagnostic questions: planning questions that reveal understanding

Use diagnostic questions when you need to see which misconception or decision is causing difficulty. A well-designed wrong option tells you something useful about students’ thinking.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
LP05 · Lesson Preparation

Scaffolding: preparing support and deciding when to remove it

Use a scaffold when a specific barrier prevents students from attempting the intended learning successfully. Keep the goal clear and plan how students will work without the support.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
CC01 · Climate & Culture

Entry routines: establishing a purposeful start

Use the agreed BSCS entry routine to make the move from corridor to independent learning warm, predictable and purposeful. Students should know where to go, what to prepare and how to begin.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
CC02 · Climate & Culture

Teaching and rehearsing classroom routines

Use this when a repeated classroom process is unreliable. Routines become useful when students understand, practise and rehearse the exact actions, rather than hear a rule once.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
CC03 · Climate & Culture

Signal for attention: securing readiness before teaching

Use the agreed BSCS signal before instructions, explanations and transitions. Secure readiness before speaking so the beginning of the message reaches the whole class.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
CC04 · Climate & Culture

Checks for listening: instructions, explanations and classmates

Use brief checks to establish whether students heard the instruction, key explanation point or contribution from a classmate. This helps distinguish missed information from difficulty understanding it.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
CC05 · Climate & Culture

Behaviour scripts: correcting calmly and precisely

Use calm, precise behaviour language to restore learning while preserving relationships. Apply the school behaviour system consistently and keep the response focused on the action that needs to change.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
CC06 · Climate & Culture

Exit routines: ending lessons calmly and efficiently

Use the agreed BSCS exit sequence to finish learning, restore the room and move students calmly into the corridor. Plan sufficient time for practical equipment and resource return.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
DN01 · Do Now

Do Now: preparing students for learning

At BSCS, Do Now provides a short, independent start using spaced retrieval of previously taught, curriculum-critical knowledge. Keep the routine stable so thinking begins without a fresh explanation.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
DN02 · Do Now

Retrieval practice: strengthening recall

Use retrieval practice to strengthen access to previously taught knowledge. Students should attempt to generate the answer from memory before they see notes, prompts or the solution.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
DN03 · Do Now

Spaced retrieval: revisiting knowledge over time

Use spaced retrieval when students can answer soon after teaching but struggle weeks later. Plan repeated returns to important knowledge rather than treating a topic as finished.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
DN04 · Do Now

Low-stakes quizzes: making retrieval accessible and challenging

Use a recurring low-stakes quiz to revisit knowledge across topics and identify what each student needs to retrieve again. The review matters as much as the score.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
DN05 · Do Now

Do Now feedback: checking responses and addressing gaps

Use a proportionate review so Do Now both strengthens recall and informs teaching. Gather the answers first, then decide which items need confirmation, discussion or a brief repair.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
EX01 · Explain

Small steps: explaining new ideas in manageable chunks

Use small steps when several interacting decisions make new content hard to follow. Teach a coherent component, rehearse it and then connect it to the next part.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
EX02 · Explain

The visualiser: live modelling step by step

Use the visualiser to show how a response is constructed, including decisions, annotations and revisions. Students see the sequence that a finished example can hide.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
EX03 · Explain

Think aloud: making expert thinking visible

Use a think aloud when the important learning sits in the choices an expert makes. Show how you plan, monitor and evaluate, including why you reject an attractive alternative.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
EX04 · Explain

Examples and non-examples: clarifying what counts

Use examples and non-examples to make the defining feature of a concept clear. Carefully chosen near-misses help students stop relying on superficial appearance.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
EX05 · Explain

Dual coding: using diagrams and words together

Use words and visuals together when a diagram makes a relationship, sequence or structure easier to understand. Select the representation for its explanatory purpose.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
EX06 · Explain

Explicit vocabulary teaching: developing keystone vocabulary

Use explicit vocabulary teaching when disciplinary language is essential to understanding and expressing an idea. Students need to hear, say, use and revisit the word in context.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
EX07 · Explain

I Do We Do You Do: moving towards independence

Use I Do, We Do, You Do to move students from observing a clear model to accurate independence. The phases may repeat; readiness determines the handover.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
PR01 · Secure Learning Through Practice

Guided practice: checking readiness for independent work

Use guided practice when students have seen an explanation but are not yet ready to perform independently. Keep the demand closely aligned with the model and inspect each important decision.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
PR02 · Secure Learning Through Practice

Completion problems: bridging modelling and independence

Use completion problems to bridge a full worked example and an independent solution. Keep part of the successful structure visible while students supply the missing decisions.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
PR03 · Secure Learning Through Practice

Fading scaffolds: removing support as students become secure

Use fading to move students beyond dependence on prompts, models or frames. Decide which support to remove from evidence of what students can now do.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
PR04 · Secure Learning Through Practice

Fluency practice: securing the essential steps

Use fluency practice when students understand a process but perform it slowly or inconsistently. Secure accuracy before increasing pace, volume or complexity.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
PR05 · Secure Learning Through Practice

Variation: changing examples to deepen understanding

Use variation to help students notice the structure of an idea rather than copy surface features. Decide what changes, what stays the same and why that comparison matters.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
PR06 · Secure Learning Through Practice

Interleaving: practising how to choose an approach

Use interleaving when students can perform several approaches separately but need practice deciding which one fits. Mix types that require a meaningful choice after initial teaching.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
PR07 · Secure Learning Through Practice

Independent practice: helping students begin and sustain effort

Use independent practice to build accurate, sustained performance after explanation and guided rehearsal. Plan the launch, first items and monitoring so students remain thinking throughout.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
DT01 · Drive Thinking for All

Wait time: giving everyone time to think

Use wait time to give everyone a chance to retrieve, reason and prepare an answer. Include a pause after a student response before immediately evaluating or asking someone else.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
DT02 · Drive Thinking for All

Cold calling: involving everyone in questioning

Use cold calling to make classroom questions an invitation for everyone to think. Build a warm, predictable question–pause–name routine and use answers to guide teaching.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
DT03 · Drive Thinking for All

Think Pair Share: preparing everyone to answer

Use Think–Pair–Share when students need independent thinking and private rehearsal before a public response. Protect the Think stage so the quickest speaker does not supply everyone’s first idea.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
DT04 · Drive Thinking for All

Turn and Talk: structuring purposeful partner discussion

Use Turn and Talk for a short, purposeful exchange that helps students clarify or rehearse an idea. Specify the question, partner roles, time and response you will collect afterwards.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
DT05 · Drive Thinking for All

Choral response: rehearsing brief answers together

Use choral response for brief, unambiguous answers that benefit from shared rehearsal. Teach a precise cue so students begin together rather than copying the earliest voice.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
DT06 · Drive Thinking for All

Probing questions: moving beyond the first answer

Use probing questions after students have relevant knowledge to deepen or clarify the reasoning behind an answer. Plan a focused follow-up rather than asking a vague “Why?” every time.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
DT07 · Drive Thinking for All

Compare justify evaluate: questions that deepen reasoning

Use comparison, justification and evaluation prompts when students need to explain a relationship or make a judgement. Ensure they have the knowledge and criteria required to reason well.

CA01 · Check & Adapt

Mini-whiteboards: checking everyone's understanding

Make every student’s answer visible, identify gaps and decide what to teach next. Useful before independent practice or whenever answers from a few students leave you unsure about everyone else.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
CA02 · Check & Adapt

Hinge questions: deciding whether to move on

Use a hinge question at a decision point where students’ answers should change what happens next. Plan the question and the teaching response together.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
CA03 · Check & Adapt

Checking for understanding during explanations

Use checks during and between explanation chunks to find out what students can recall, distinguish or apply. Gather evidence that informs a specific teaching decision.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
CA04 · Check & Adapt

Circulation: sampling independent work and responding

Use circulation to read learning across the room, identify the exact error and choose a response. Move with a route and a diagnostic focus rather than following raised hands alone.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
CA05 · Check & Adapt

Exit tickets: identifying what needs revisiting

Use an exit ticket when a brief independent response can inform the next lesson. Choose essential knowledge and a format that can be reviewed quickly.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
CA06 · Check & Adapt

Pause and Fix: responding to a common misconception

Use Pause & Fix when a common gap means continuing would reinforce an error or make the next step inaccessible. Stop briefly, repair the precise issue and return to a fresh attempt.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
CA07 · Check & Adapt

Adapt and Support Extend and Challenge: responding to different needs

Use Adapt & Support and Extend & Challenge when responses show different needs. Keep the learning goal ambitious while adjusting the support or depth of the next task.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
FI01 · Feedback to Improve

Actionable feedback: giving students a useful next step

Use individual feedback when a precise next action can improve work while the thinking is still live. Make the location, learning issue and required change clear.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
FI02 · Feedback to Improve

Whole-class feedback: responding to patterns in work

Use whole-class feedback when students’ work reveals shared strengths and recurring difficulties. Review the pattern once, then give everyone a useful improvement task.

Read guide →PDF ↗Word ↓
FI03 · Feedback to Improve

Self-checking: teaching students to improve their own work

Use self-checking when students know what quality looks like but do not yet inspect their own work reliably. Teach a specific checking action rather than telling them to “check it”.

FI04 · Feedback to Improve

Peer critique: using criteria to improve work

Use peer critique when students understand the content and criteria well enough to offer accurate, useful feedback. Teach the feedback routine before exchanging work.

FI05 · Feedback to Improve

Feedback tasks: planning time to act on feedback

Use feedback tasks to make improvement an act of thinking. Select a solvable challenge that helps students locate, explain and repair an issue rather than simply copy a correction.

FI06 · Feedback to Improve

Feedback follow-up: checking improvement on a new task

Use feedback follow-up to find out whether the learning improved beyond the original correction. A new attempt gives more useful evidence than a rewritten answer alone.

EX08 · Explain

Worked examples: showing a complete solution

Use a worked example when students need to see the full structure of a successful response before attempting a complex task. Make the important decisions and criteria visible.

FI07 · Feedback to Improve

The visualiser: discussing and improving student work

Use the visualiser to make student work a shared learning resource. Select a response because it illustrates a useful success, misconception or improvement decision.

CC07 · Climate & Culture

Clear instructions and front-loading: specify participation before the task

Use front-loading when students begin responding or moving before they have heard the participation instructions. Say how to respond before giving the content that will capture attention.

CC08 · Climate & Culture

Habits of attention: teaching purposeful listening routines

Use habits of attention to teach where students should direct attention during explanation, modelling and discussion. Each habit needs a learning purpose and a recognisable cue.

CC09 · Climate & Culture

Classroom transitions: moving smoothly between learning activities

Use a taught transition to move students from one activity to the next without losing attention or learning time. Specify how to stop, shift resources and begin the new demand.

CC10 · Climate & Culture

Precorrections: preventing predictable problems before they start

Use a precorrection when a predictable situation repeatedly produces the same difficulty. Prompt the desired action immediately before that moment, using the pattern you have noticed.

CC11 · Climate & Culture

Making participation safe: prepare, rehearse and respond warmly

Use safe participation routines when fear of public error prevents students from contributing. Pair challenge with preparation and respond to uncertainty in predictable, respectful ways.

DT08 · Drive Thinking for All

Everyone–Together–Anyone: planning participation for the whole class

Use Everyone–Together–Anyone to plan how all students think, rehearse and remain accountable. Choose a participation sequence that serves the learning rather than rely on confident volunteers.

DT09 · Drive Thinking for All

Second Chance / No Opt Out: returning after ‘I don’t know’

Use Second Chance when a student’s first response is “I don’t know” or incomplete. Provide a route to a successful contribution and return to the student.

DT10 · Drive Thinking for All

Oracy for learning: teaching speaking and listening explicitly

Use oracy routines to teach speaking and listening as skills that support disciplinary thinking. Clarify whether students are exploring an idea or presenting a developed explanation.

DT11 · Drive Thinking for All

Everybody Writes / Silent Solo: thinking in writing before discussion

Use Everybody Writes or Silent Solo when students need to form their own response before discussion. Writing gives quieter students a prepared idea and makes initial thinking visible.

EX09 · Explain

Explaining with precision: plan, sequence and rehearse the explanation

Use precise explanation when the content is correct but the message is too long, unclear or difficult to follow. Plan what to say, what to show and what to leave out.

EX10 · Explain

Cognitive simplicity: designing slides and resources that support attention

Use cognitive simplicity when slides or resources compete with the explanation. Reduce unnecessary searching, reading and distraction so students can attend to the content that matters.

Live drawing: building a representation step by step

Use live drawing to build a representation in the same sequence as the explanation. Clarity and purpose matter more than artistic polish.

Storytelling and analogies: making an explanation coherent and memorable

Use a story or analogy when it clarifies a sequence, relationship or abstract idea. Keep the narrative tied to the disciplinary meaning students must learn.

CA08 · Check & Adapt

Micro-decisions: notice, interpret and respond in the moment

Use micro-decisions to make teaching responsive while the lesson is unfolding. Notice a useful signal, interpret its likely cause and choose a proportionate next action.

CA09 · Check & Adapt

High success rates: deciding when students are ready for independence

Use success-rate evidence to judge whether practice is productive and students are ready for greater independence. Interpret accuracy alongside reasoning, task demand and the distribution of errors.

LP06 · Lesson Preparation

Atomisation: breaking learning into prerequisite and new knowledge

Use atomisation in lesson preparation to identify the small pieces of knowledge and action a successful performance requires. Separate existing prerequisites from genuinely new learning.

CA10 · Check & Adapt

Walking-talking mocks: attempt, diagnose, model and re-check

Use an active walking-talking mock to combine expert modelling with student attempts and diagnosis. Give explanation time where the responses show it is needed.

Review Cards: turning errors into future retrieval

Use Review Cards to turn corrected errors into a personal retrieval resource. Separate the question from the solution so students can attempt it again without seeing the answer.

‘What if?’ questions: vary a condition to deepen understanding

Use What If questions to deepen a secure example by changing one condition. Students should adapt the reasoning they have established rather than begin an unrelated problem.

Golden Silence and active observation: launching independent practice

Use confidence scores alongside answers to identify uncertainty and confidently held errors. Confidence adds context to performance; it does not replace evidence of knowledge.

Learner-generated examples: testing concept boundaries

Use learner-generated examples to test the boundaries of a concept. Constraints help students move beyond the first obvious example and expose what they think counts.

Consolidation: securing new learning before independent practice

Use consolidation after initial explanation and guided practice to secure the new idea before increasing independence or complexity. Make students reconstruct and explain the learning.

PR11 · Secure Learning Through Practice

Problem-solving: applying secure knowledge in less familiar tasks

Use problem-solving to help students apply secure knowledge when the route is less familiar. Plan the extra decision demand rather than disguise new teaching inside a complex task.

LP07 · Lesson Preparation

Purpose: helping students understand what they are learning and why

Use a clear purpose to help students understand what the lesson is building towards and why the learning matters. Connect activities to the knowledge, performance or later use.

Retrieval homework: revisiting learning beyond the lesson

Use retrieval homework to revisit taught knowledge between lessons. Make the independent attempt possible, provide useful feedback and connect gaps to future teaching.
